l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: The Lion is delighted to leave city life and return to the country, where he hopes to show the other beasts how courageous he has become. He helps recognize that the trees are fighting them and stopping their journey.

l: Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Dorothy thinks Oz was not such a bad Wizard after all because he did his best and gave the Scarecrow brains and the Lion courage. Although he did not keep his promise to Dorothy, she forgives him and considers him a good man, even if he was a bad Wizard.

l: Emerald City, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Dorothy and her companions leave the Emerald City and look back at its green walls, towers, steeples, and the spires and dome of Oz's Palace. The Scarecrow is expected to return because he is now its ruler.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Kansas is the place Dorothy hopes to return to. She continues traveling toward the Land of the South in order to find a way home.

l: fighting trees, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: The first row of trees in the forest attacks strangers by bending and twining its branches around them. The Tin Woodman cuts one tree's branch, after which the travelers can pass; they believe these trees act as policemen of the forest to keep strangers out.

l: forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: The travelers enter a thick forest because it extends too far to go around and they fear getting lost if they change direction. The first row of trees attacks them, but the rest of the forest allows them to pass until they reach its farther edge.

l: white china wall, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: At the far edge of the forest, the travelers find a high wall made of white china. It is smooth like the surface of a dish and higher than their heads, so the Tin Woodman plans to make a ladder to climb over it.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XIX
s: Dorothy and her companions continue their journey toward the Land of the South so she can return to Kansas. They travel through fields and a forest, overcome the attacking trees, and reach a white china wall that blocks their way.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: Dorothy, the Tin Woodman, the Scarecrow, the Lion, and Toto enter the Dainty China Country after climbing a wall. They find a tiny country of china houses, animals, and people, and must cross it carefully because its inhabitants can break easily. Dorothy meets a china Princess, who explains that china people become stiff when taken away from their country. The travelers reach the far wall, but the Lion accidentally smashes a china church while jumping onto it.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: Dorothy sleeps while the Tin Woodman makes a ladder, then climbs over the wall with the others. She apologizes after a china cow breaks its leg and meets a china Princess, whom she offers to carry back to Kansas before learning that the Princess would become stiff and unhappy away from her country. Dorothy helps the group cross the china country carefully.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The Tin Woodman makes a ladder from wood found in the forest so the group can climb the wall. He climbs over the wall last and helps the others cross the china country, warning that they may hurt its inhabitants.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The Scarecrow watches the Tin Woodman make the ladder and climbs it first. He falls from the wall so the others can jump onto him, flattening his body, but they pat his straw back into shape. He is thankful that being made of straw keeps him from being easily damaged.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The Lion sleeps before climbing the wall and later helps the group reach the far wall. When he jumps onto it, his tail upsets a china church and smashes it.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: Toto climbs over the wall after the Scarecrow and begins to bark at the strange country, but Dorothy makes him be quiet. He crosses the china country with the others.

l: The Dainty China Country, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The Dainty China Country has a smooth, shining white floor and small houses, barns, fences, animals, and people made entirely of china. Its inhabitants live contentedly there, but they become stiff when taken away from the country.

l: china people, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The china people include milkmaids, shepherdesses, princesses, shepherds, princes, and clowns, all made of china and small enough that the tallest is no higher than Dorothy's knee. They fear being broken, and damaged china people can be glued or mended but may no longer look as pretty.

l: china Princess, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The china Princess runs from Dorothy because she fears falling and breaking herself. She explains that china people can be mended but are never as pretty afterward, and that those taken away from their country become stiff and can only stand straight and look pretty.

l: ladder, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The Tin Woodman makes a clumsy but strong ladder from forest wood. The group uses it to climb the first wall, but they cannot pull it up afterward and leave it behind.

l: wall, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The travelers climb over a high wall to enter the Dainty China Country. They later reach another, lower wall on the far side and climb over it by standing on the Lion's back.

l: crossing the china country, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: Dorothy and the others cross the china country carefully so they will not break its people or animals. They reach the opposite wall after about an hour, having caused a china cow's leg to break and a china church to be smashed.

l: china people's brittleness, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XX
s: The china people and animals can break from falls, kicks, or other accidents. Broken parts may be glued or mended, but the repaired china person may be cracked and less pretty than before.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The travelers cross a disagreeable country and enter a vast, ancient forest. There they meet hundreds of forest animals threatened by a giant spider that has killed the other lions. The Lion defeats the spider by striking off its head while it sleeps. The animals make him their King, and he promises to rule them after Dorothy is safely on her way to Kansas.

l: the travelers' party, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The travelers cross bogs, marshes, tall grass, underbrush, and a forest before stopping to sleep. They continue along a well-trodden path and meet hundreds of animals gathered in a forest opening.

l: forest (the Lion's forest), The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The forest is older and wilder than any the travelers have seen, with large trees, soft dried leaves, and rich green moss. A giant spider has entered it and threatens all the animals living there.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The Lion enjoys the forest and is not afraid when the animals gather there. He agrees to fight their enemy, defeats the great spider, and is made King of the Forest.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: Dorothy travels through the boggy country and forest with her companions. She is briefly afraid when she sees the hundreds of animals, but the Lion explains that they are holding a meeting.

l: beasts of the forest, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The forest animals gather to discuss the danger posed by a giant spider that eats them. After the Lion kills the spider, they bow down to him as their King.

l: tiger, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The biggest of the tigers welcomes the Lion as King of Beasts and explains the animals' trouble. He promises, along with the other animals, to obey the Lion if he destroys the great spider.

l: great spider, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The great spider is a tremendous monster with an elephant-sized body, eight long legs, coarse black hair, and sharp teeth. It has killed all the other lions in the forest, but the Lion knocks its head from its body while it sleeps.

l: Lion's battle with the spider, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: The Lion finds the great spider asleep and notices that its head is connected to its body by a slender neck. He jumps onto its back and knocks off its head with one blow of his clawed paw, killing it.

l: the animals' submission to the Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: After the great spider is killed, the forest animals bow down to the Lion as their King. The Lion promises to return and rule them after Dorothy is safely on her way to Kansas.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXI
s: Kansas remains Dorothy's destination. The Lion says he will return to rule the forest animals once Dorothy is safely on her way there.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The four travelers reach a steep hill guarded by hundreds of armless Hammer-Heads, whose shooting heads knock down the Scarecrow and the Lion. Dorothy summons the Winged Monkeys, who carry the travelers and Toto over the hill for the last time. In the country of the Quadlings, the travelers receive food and directions to the Castle of Glinda, where they are admitted to see Glinda.

l: the travelers' party, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The four travelers cross the forest, are carried over the Hammer-Heads’ hill by the Winged Monkeys, and arrive safely in the country of the Quadlings. They eat at a farmhouse and continue walking to the Castle of Glinda.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The Scarecrow leads the travelers toward the hill despite a warning from the Hammer-Heads. A Hammer-Head strikes him with its extended head and sends him tumbling down the hill.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The Lion attacks the Hammer-Heads after they laugh at the Scarecrow, but a shooting head knocks him down the hill. He concludes that no one can withstand the Hammer-Heads by fighting them.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: Dorothy helps the Scarecrow after he is knocked down and asks what the travelers can do against the Hammer-Heads. She summons the Winged Monkeys, travels with the others to the country of the Quadlings, and is admitted to the Castle of Glinda.

l: Hammer-Heads, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The Hammer-Heads guard the steep hill and refuse to let the travelers cross. They have no arms but can shoot and stretch their heads forward with enough force to knock down the Scarecrow and the Lion; they cannot reach the Winged Monkeys in flight.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The Winged Monkeys answer Dorothy’s summons and carry the four travelers and Toto over the hill to the country of the Quadlings. Their leader tells Dorothy that this is the last time she can summon them before they depart.

l: Land of the South, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The country of the Quadlings is rich and happy, with fields of grain, paved roads, brooks, and bridges. Its fences, houses, and bridges are red, and its short, fat inhabitants wear red clothing.

l: hill, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The hill is steep and covered from top to bottom with large pieces of rock. It belongs to the Hammer-Heads, who prevent the travelers from crossing it until the Winged Monkeys carry them over.

l: Castle of Glinda, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The Castle of Glinda is a beautiful castle in the country of the Quadlings. Three young girls in red uniforms guard its gates, and Dorothy and the others are admitted at once.

l: Glinda, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: Glinda is the Good Witch who rules the South Country. A girl soldier asks Glinda whether she will receive Dorothy and the others, and returns with permission for them to enter the Castle.

l: crossing the hill, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: The travelers cannot cross the hill by climbing because the Hammer-Heads knock down the Scarecrow and the Lion. They cross it when the Winged Monkeys carry them over the hill.

l: summoning the Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXII
s: Dorothy uses the Golden Cap and speaks the magic words to summon the Winged Monkeys. They arrive promptly, fulfill her command to carry the travelers over the hill, and then tell her that she cannot summon them again.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy and her companions visit Glinda the Good Witch, who agrees to help Dorothy return to Kansas in exchange for the Golden Cap. Glinda arranges for the Winged Monkeys to carry the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Lion to the places where they wish to live. She explains that Dorothy’s Silver Shoes can carry her anywhere in three steps. Dorothy uses them to return to Kansas, but the shoes fall off and are lost in the desert.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy tells Glinda the Good Witch about her arrival in the Land of Oz and her adventures with her companions. She gives Glinda the Golden Cap, says goodbye to her friends, and uses the Silver Shoes to return to Kansas.

l: Glinda, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Glinda agrees to tell Dorothy how to return to Kansas in exchange for the Golden Cap. She promises to send the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, and Lion to their desired homes with the Winged Monkeys, and explains the power of the Silver Shoes.

l: Scarecrow, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Scarecrow plans to return to the Emerald City, where Oz has made him ruler. Glinda promises that the Winged Monkeys will carry him over the hill of the Hammer-Heads to the Emerald City.

l: Tin Woodman, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Tin Woodman wishes to return to the Country of the West and rule the Winkies. Glinda promises that the Winged Monkeys will carry him safely to the land of the Winkies.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Lion wishes to return to the forest beyond the hill of the Hammer-Heads, where the beasts have made him their King. Glinda promises that the Winged Monkeys will carry him there.

l: Aunt Em, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Aunt Em is waiting in Kansas and will think something dreadful has happened to Dorothy if Dorothy does not return. Dorothy asks the Silver Shoes to take her home to Aunt Em.

l: Winged Monkeys, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Winged Monkeys are to carry the Scarecrow to the Emerald City, the Tin Woodman to the land of the Winkies, and the Lion to his forest. After Glinda uses the Golden Cap’s powers three times, she will give it to the King of the Monkeys so the Winged Monkeys can be free forevermore.

l: Land of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Land of Oz is the country Dorothy has traveled through after the cyclone brought her there. Dorothy leaves it when the Silver Shoes carry her back to Kansas.

l: Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Kansas is Dorothy’s home. The Silver Shoes carry her there, and she arrives on the prairie near the new farmhouse Uncle Henry built.

l: Golden Cap, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy gives the Golden Cap to Glinda because it is no longer useful to her. Glinda uses its three commands to send the Winged Monkeys to carry Dorothy’s companions to their chosen destinations.

l: Silver Shoes, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: The Silver Shoes can carry Dorothy anywhere in the world in three steps, with each step taking place in the wink of an eye. Dorothy knocks their heels together three times and reaches Kansas, but the shoes fall off during the flight and are lost forever in the desert.

l: Dorothy's journey through Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy tells Glinda about the cyclone that brought her to the Land of Oz, the companions she found, and the wonderful adventures they experienced. Her journey gives the Scarecrow brains, the Tin Woodman a heart, and the Lion courage.

l: Dorothy's return to Kansas, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy says goodbye to Glinda the Good Witch and her companions before using the Silver Shoes to return to Kansas. She arrives on the broad Kansas prairie near Uncle Henry’s new farmhouse with Toto.

l: Dorothy's greatest wish, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIII
s: Dorothy’s greatest wish is to get back to Kansas so that Aunt Em will not think something dreadful has happened to her. Glinda tells her that the Silver Shoes can fulfill this wish.

l: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: Aunt Em comes out of the house to water the cabbages and sees Dorothy running toward her. Aunt Em embraces Dorothy and kisses her, asking where she came from. Dorothy says she has returned from the Land of Oz with Toto and is glad to be home again.

l: Aunt Em, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: Aunt Em is watering the cabbages when she sees Dorothy running toward her. She embraces Dorothy, covers her face with kisses, and asks where she came from.

l: Dorothy, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: Dorothy returns from the Land of Oz with Toto. She tells Aunt Em that she is glad to be home again.

l: Toto, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: Toto returns with Dorothy from the Land of Oz.

l: Land of Oz, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: The Land of Oz is the place Dorothy says she has come from.

l: home (Dorothy's home), The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Chapter XXIV
s: Dorothy returns home and says she is glad to be there again.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: L. Frank Baum explains that he wrote The Marvelous Land of Oz after receiving many letters from children asking for more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman. He says he promised a little girl named Dorothy that he would write the book after receiving a thousand such letters, and he dedicates the book to David C. Montgomery and Frank A. Stone. The text includes a list of chapters concerning characters and events in the land of Oz, including Tip, Pumpkinhead, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, Old Mombi, Glinda the Good, and Princess Ozma of Oz.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Marvelous Land of Oz is the book L. Frank Baum says he wrote after promising to answer children's requests for more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.

l: L. Frank Baum, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: L. Frank Baum explains that children's letters led him to write The Marvelous Land of Oz. He says he dedicated the book to David C. Montgomery and Frank A. Stone.

l: Dorothy, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Dorothy is identified as the little girl who made a long journey to see L. Frank Baum and asked him to write more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Scarecrow is one of the characters about whom children asked L. Frank Baum to write more. He appears in the chapter list as a character who plans an escape, takes time to think, and appeals to Glinda the Good.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Tin Woodman is one of the characters about whom children repeatedly asked L. Frank Baum to write more.

l: children, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Children sent L. Frank Baum letters expressing their pleasure in reading The Wonderful Wizard of OZ and asking for more about the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman.

l: letters, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Letters from children continued to reach L. Frank Baum for months and years. After he promised to write the book when a thousand little girls had asked for it, the thousand letters and many more arrived.

l: the stage production of “The Wizard of OZ”, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The success of the stage production of “The Wizard of OZ” is suggested by L. Frank Baum as one reason new friends may have joined the story and helped bring the thousand letters.

l: Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The land of Oz is the setting named in the title and chapter list.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Tip appears in the chapter list as the character who manufactures Pumpkinhead and makes an experiment in magic.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Pumpkinhead appears in the chapter list as a figure manufactured by Tip.

l: Powder of Life, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Marvelous Powder of Life is named as the subject of a chapter.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Saw-horse appears in the chapter list as a character or object that is awakened.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Emerald City appears in the chapter list as the destination of Jack Pumpkinhead's ride.

l: Queen Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Gen. Jinjur appears in the chapter list in connection with an army of revolt.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Gen. Jinjur's Army of Revolt is named in the chapter list.

l: the Tin-Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Tin-Woodman appears in the chapter list as a figure whom the Scarecrow travels to meet and who plucks a rose.

l: Woggle-Bug, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E. is named in the chapter list.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Old Mombi appears in the chapter list as a character who indulges in witchcraft and is later transformed.

l: Gump, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: The Gump appears in the chapter list in connection with an astonishing flight.

l: Dr. Nikidik, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Dr. Nikidik appears in the chapter list as the maker or possessor of famous wishing pills.

l: Glinda the Good, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Glinda the Good appears in the chapter list as the person to whom the Scarecrow appeals.

l: Princess Ozma, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz
s: Princess Ozma of Oz is named in the chapter list in a chapter titled with her transformation or appearance.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead
s: Tip is a youth raised by the sorceress Mombi in the Country of the Gillikins. While Mombi is away, Tip carves a pumpkin face, builds a wooden body, and dresses it in clothing taken from Mombi’s chest. He names his creation Jack Pumpkinhead and plans to use it to frighten Mombi.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead
s: Tip is a strong, rugged youth raised by Mombi, whom he openly hates despite her being his guardian. While Mombi is away for two days, he makes a wooden man with a carved pumpkin head, dresses it in colorful clothing, and names it Jack Pumpkinhead.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead
s: Mombi is Tip’s guardian and is suspected by her neighbors of practicing magical arts. She leaves for a village to buy groceries, giving Tip time to construct Jack Pumpkinhead, and Tip intends to frighten her with the figure when she returns.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead
s: Jack Pumpkinhead is the name Tip gives to the tall wooden man he constructs with a carved, smiling pumpkin for a head. The figure has jointed arms and legs, a wooden neck, and clothing taken from Mombi’s belongings and Tip’s shoes.

l: Tip’s manufacture of Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Manufactures a Pumpkinhead
s: Tip carves a large orange-red pumpkin into a face with round eyes, a three-cornered nose, and a broad smiling mouth. He cuts saplings for the limbs, fashions a bark cylinder for the body, adds a wooden neck and joints, and dresses the figure in purple trousers, a red shirt, a spotted pink vest, stockings, and shoes.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Tip places Jack Pumpkinhead at a bend in the road and repairs him after his arm falls off and his head twists around. Mombi returns with new magical supplies, uses the Powder of Life to animate Jack, and takes him home with Tip. Mombi then prepares a potion of milk, vinegar, herbs, and powders that she intends to make Tip drink so he will be transformed into a marble statue. Tip remains awake after Mombi locks the potion in her room, fearing what will happen at daybreak.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Tip carries Jack Pumpkinhead to a bend in the road, repairs his detached arm with a stronger pin, and turns his pumpkin head to face forward. He secretly watches Mombi sprinkle the Powder of Life over Jack and is amazed when Jack comes to life. Mombi threatens to transform Tip into a marble statue, but he stays awake rather than going to bed while she prepares the potion.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Jack Pumpkinhead is positioned by Tip at the bend in the road as a dummy. After Mombi sprinkles the Powder of Life over him and performs an incantation, he comes to life and speaks, walks, and considers whether he is wise or foolish. Mombi takes him home and locks him in an empty stall in the cow stable.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Mombi returns home with magical recipes, powders, and herbs obtained through a trade with a crooked wizard. She uses the Powder of Life to animate Jack Pumpkinhead, then confines him in the cow stable. She prepares a potion intended to transform Tip into a marble statue and plans to complete the transformation at daybreak.

l: Powder of Life, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: The Powder of Life is kept by Mombi in an old pepper-box labeled by a wizard. Mombi sprinkles it over Jack Pumpkinhead and uses three shouted magical words, after which Jack comes to life.

l: the transformation potion, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Mombi prepares the transformation potion in a small black kettle from equal parts milk and vinegar, along with herbs and powders measured according to a recipe. She tells Tip that, if properly made, it will transform him into a marble statue. The potion must cool overnight before Tip drinks it.

l: the marble statue, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Mombi intends the marble statue to be Tip after his threatened transformation. She plans to place him in the middle of a flower garden as an ornament.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead's animation, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Jack Pumpkinhead's animation occurs when Mombi sprinkles the Powder of Life over his pumpkin head and clothing and performs the required incantation. He immediately steps back, complains that Mombi is yelling, and demonstrates that he can speak and walk.

l: Tip's threatened transformation, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Powder of Life
s: Mombi threatens to transform Tip into a marble statue because she wants to punish him and no longer tolerate his troublesome behavior. She prepares the potion for this purpose and says she will complete the transformation at daybreak. Tip is frightened, protests that he does not want to become a marble statue, and remains awake after Mombi locks the potion away.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: Tip escapes from Mombi’s house after taking bread, cheese, and the Powder of Life because he fears being turned into a marble statue. He frees Jack Pumpkinhead, and the two travel south toward the Emerald City. Along the way, Tip explains the history and rulers of the Land of Oz to Jack, including the Scarecrow’s rule of the Emerald City.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: Tip decides to run away from Mombi rather than become a marble statue. He takes food and the Powder of Life, frees Jack Pumpkinhead, and travels with him toward the Emerald City.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: Mombi is asleep when Tip leaves her house. Tip believes she intends to turn him into a marble statue and takes the Powder of Life so she cannot use it to make more mischief.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: Jack Pumpkinhead leaves Mombi’s cow-stable with Tip and travels south with him. He learns that Tip made him and accepts Tip as his creator and father, owing him obedience while expecting support.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: The Emerald City is described as the center of the Land of Oz and the biggest town in the country. Everything there is green, and the Scarecrow rules it as King after the Wizard escaped in a balloon.

l: Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: The Land of Oz contains the Emerald City and four colored countries: the purple Country of the Gillikins, the blue Country of the Munchkins, the red country of the Quadlings, and the yellow country of the Winkies. Tip explains that the Scarecrow rules the Emerald City, the Tin Woodman rules the Winkies, and Glinda the Good rules the Quadlings.

l: flight from Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Flight of the Fugitives
s: Tip begins his flight from Mombi by leaving her house at night with bread, cheese, and the Powder of Life. He brings Jack Pumpkinhead with him, takes winding paths to make pursuit difficult, and travels toward the Emerald City.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: Tip travels with Jack Pumpkinhead, whose wooden joints are weak and wear out when he walks or sits. After Jack points out that a wooden sawhorse resembles a real horse, Tip decides to use the Powder of Life on it so Jack can ride it. Tip imitates Mombi’s words and gestures while sprinkling powder from the pepper-box, and the saw-horse comes to life.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: Tip worries about Jack Pumpkinhead’s weak wooden joints and tries to find a way to remedy them. He uses the Powder of Life from the pepper-box on the saw-horse, imitating Mombi’s words and gestures, and successfully brings it to life.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: Jack Pumpkinhead’s wooden joints give way when he tries to sit down, so Tip tells him to remain standing. He suggests riding the saw-horse if it can be brought to life, and watches as Tip’s experiment succeeds.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: Mombi is identified as the person whose words and hand movements Tip imitates when he performs the magic that brings the saw-horse to life.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: The saw-horse is a wooden structure made from a tree trunk, branches, knots, and four wooden legs, used for sawing logs. After Tip sprinkles it with the Powder of Life and repeats Mombi’s spell, it moves, stretches its legs, yawns, and shakes powder from its back.

l: Powder of Life, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: The Powder of Life is sprinkled from the pepper-box onto the saw-horse. It appears to vanish into the horse’s body, after which the saw-horse comes to life.

l: pepper-box, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: The pepper-box contains the magical Powder of Life. Tip takes it from his pocket and uses it to sprinkle powder on the saw-horse.

l: bringing the saw-horse to life, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: Tip attempts to bring the saw-horse to life by sprinkling it with the Powder of Life and repeating the words and gestures he remembers from Mombi. The attempt succeeds, and the saw-horse moves, stretches, yawns, and shakes off some powder.

l: magic, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Tip Makes an Experiment in Magic
s: The magic in this unit involves the Powder of Life, the pepper-box, and the spoken words and hand gestures associated with Mombi. Tip uses this magic to bring the wooden saw-horse to life.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: Tip brings the Saw-Horse to life, but the creature initially cannot control its stiff legs, hear commands, or understand its surroundings. Tip gives the Saw-Horse bark ears, teaches it commands, and equips it with a post for Jack Pumpkinhead to hold while riding. The group begins its journey to the Emerald City, following a yellow-brick roadway marked as nine miles from the city. At nightfall, Tip makes camp and asks the Saw-Horse to stand guard while he and Jack sleep.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: Tip brings the Saw-Horse to life and tries to control it after it bumps into Jack Pumpkinhead and steps on Tip’s foot. He makes bark ears for the Saw-Horse, teaches it the meanings of “Whoa,” “Get-Up,” and “Trot,” and fastens a post to its back for Jack to hold. Tip then leads the group toward the Emerald City and camps beside the road at nightfall.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: Jack Pumpkinhead is knocked down by the newly awakened Saw-Horse but takes an active interest in the creature. He suggests making ears for the Saw-Horse, helps hold its head while Tip attaches them, and rides on its back during the journey. At camp, Tip helps Jack lie on the ground to rest.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: The Saw-Horse awakens alive but has stiff, awkward legs, no ears, and difficulty understanding its surroundings. After Tip gives it ears and teaches it commands, it agrees to obey and carries Jack Pumpkinhead while walking in a rocking, side-to-side manner. It cannot sleep, so Tip leaves it standing to watch for anyone who might disturb the camp.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse begin traveling toward the Emerald City. Their path becomes a broad roadway paved with yellow brick, and a sign states that the Emerald City is nine miles away. Because darkness is approaching, Tip stops the journey and camps beside the road.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Awakening of the Saw-horse
s: The Emerald City is the destination of Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse. A roadside sign indicates that it is nine miles away, and the travelers plan to see His Majesty, the Scarecrow, there.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse resume their journey to the Emerald City and cross a broad river by using the Saw-Horse as a boat. Tip falls behind when the Saw-Horse races ahead, while Jack Pumpkinhead and the Saw-Horse reach the Emerald City. The Guardian of the Gates and the Soldier with the Green Whiskers bring Jack and the Saw-Horse into the city and escort them toward the royal palace. Jack is taken to meet the Scarecrow, who rules the Emerald City.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: Tip resumes his journey with Jack Pumpkinhead and the Saw-Horse, crossing a river by riding the Saw-Horse. When he orders the Saw-Horse to trot, it races ahead, and Tip loses his grip on its tail and is left behind. He rests, then continues walking toward the Emerald City, expecting to overtake them at the city gates.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: Jack Pumpkinhead crosses the river by holding the Saw-Horse’s tail and reaches the Emerald City after Tip is left behind. He tells the Guardian of the Gates that he does not know his business and is taken to the Scarecrow. Jack wears green spectacles and remains calm and cheerful throughout.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: The Saw-Horse floats across the river and moves its legs like oars. After Tip commands it to trot, it races along the road and carries Jack Pumpkinhead to the Emerald City. It obeys Jack’s command to stop, receives green spectacles, kicks a barking green dog, and is led around to the rear of the palace.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: The Emerald City is surrounded by a high green stone wall thickly studded with emeralds. Its streets, buildings, towers, turrets, and pavement are decorated with green gems, and its people wear or appear in green. Jack Pumpkinhead and the Saw-Horse enter the city and proceed to the royal palace.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: The Scarecrow rules the Emerald City and is seated upon a glittering throne in the royal palace. Jack Pumpkinhead is brought before him after the Soldier with the Green Whiskers decides that the Scarecrow should determine what to do with Jack.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Jack Pumpkinhead’s Ride to the Emerald City
s: The journey continues over a road of yellow brick after Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse cross a broad river. The Saw-Horse’s great speed separates Tip from the others, but Jack and the Saw-Horse reach the Emerald City and are escorted to the royal palace.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: His Majesty the Scarecrow meets Jack Pumpkinhead, who has come from the Country of the Gillikins and is surprised by the Scarecrow’s appearance. Believing they speak different languages, the Scarecrow summons an interpreter, and the Soldier with the Green Whiskers brings Jellia Jamb. Jellia reveals that all of Oz speaks one language, making an interpreter unnecessary, while amusingly mistranslating their remarks. The Scarecrow and Jack become friends and go to the courtyard to play quoits.

l: His Majesty the Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: His Majesty the Scarecrow is described as a straw-filled ruler wearing faded blue clothes, a jeweled golden crown, and a painted face. He mistakenly believes Jack Pumpkinhead speaks a different language, summons an interpreter, and then learns from Jellia Jamb that all of Oz speaks the same language. He befriends Jack and leads him to the courtyard to play quoits.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: Jack Pumpkinhead meets His Majesty the Scarecrow after coming from the Country of the Gillikins. Because his carved face is permanently smiling and his wooden body cannot bend, he is repeatedly misunderstood and teased, but he becomes friends with the Scarecrow and joins him in playing quoits.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: The Emerald City is ruled by His Majesty the Scarecrow and uses the same language spoken throughout the Land of Oz. Jack Pumpkinhead visits the city and meets the Scarecrow there.

l: Jellia Jamb, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: Jellia Jamb is brought to His Majesty the Scarecrow as a supposed interpreter because she was born in the North Country and is believed to understand the language of the Gillikins. She reveals that the Gillikins' language and the language of the Emerald City are the same, while mischievously mistranslating remarks between the Scarecrow and Jack.

l: interpreter, The Marvelous Land of Oz, His Majesty the Scarecrow
s: An interpreter is described as someone who understands and speaks both languages involved in a conversation and translates each speaker's meaning for the other. The Scarecrow believes one is needed to communicate with Jack Pumpkinhead, but Jellia Jamb shows that no interpreter is necessary because all of Oz speaks one language.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: Tip meets General Jinjur, who commands an Army of Revolt made up entirely of girls seeking to overthrow the Scarecrow and take control of the Emerald City. The army, armed with knitting-needles, marches to the city and demands its surrender. The Guardian of the Gate is overcome, and the Soldier with the Green Whiskers flees after admitting that his gun is unloaded. General Jinjur and her army capture the Emerald City without bloodshed.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: Tip meets General Jinjur while walking toward the Emerald City and accepts food from her. He follows her to the Army of Revolt, carries baskets and packages for its members, and witnesses the capture of the Emerald City.

l: General Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: General Jinjur commands the Army of Revolt and plans to overthrow the Scarecrow, seize the Emerald City’s gems and treasury, and govern the city herself. She leads the army to the city, takes the Guardian of the Gate’s keys, and directs the capture of the Emerald City.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Army of Revolt consists of about four hundred girls from all parts of the Land of Oz. Its members wear colorful uniforms and carry knitting-needles as weapons, then overcome the city’s defenders and become an Army of Conquerors.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Emerald City is the target of General Jinjur’s revolt because it contains beautiful gems and a royal treasury. Its gateway is entered by the Army of Revolt, which captures the city without bloodshed.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Scarecrow is the king ruling the Emerald City. General Jinjur’s army intends to dethrone him, and his Royal Army is described as old, feeble, and ineffective.

l: Guardian of the Gates of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Guardian of the Gate initially treats General Jinjur’s army as harmless visitors and tells them to go home. The girls surround him with knitting-needles, causing him to surrender and allowing General Jinjur to take his keys.

l: the Soldier with the Green Whiskers, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Soldier with the Green Whiskers is the Royal Army of Oz and comes to defend the Emerald City. He reveals that his gun is not loaded, then runs through the gate toward the royal palace when the girls attack.

l: the war between Glinda and Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The war is a secret conflict planned by General Jinjur’s army against the men of Oz and the rule of the Scarecrow. General Jinjur claims it will be pleasant because she believes no man will harm a girl.

l: the Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The Revolt is General Jinjur’s uprising against male rule in Oz. Its stated aims are to conquer the Emerald City, dethrone the Scarecrow, obtain the city’s gems and treasury, and gain power for the girls.

l: Jinjur's takeover of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Gen. Jinjur’s Army of Revolt
s: The conquest of the Emerald City is achieved when General Jinjur’s army enters through the gateway after defeating the city’s ineffective defenders. The city is captured without a drop of blood being spilled.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: Tip follows the Soldier with the Green Whiskers into the conquered Emerald City and warns the Scarecrow that the invading girls plan to use his straw and stuffing. The Scarecrow, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Soldier decide to escape on the Saw-Horse and ride toward the Tin Woodman’s kingdom. They break through the palace guards and the city gate, but the Saw-Horse carries them to a wide river and leaps into the water.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: Tip follows the Soldier with the Green Whiskers into the Emerald City and reaches the palace. He warns the Scarecrow that the invading girls intend to make a rag carpet from his outside and stuff sofa-cushions with his inside. Tip rides at the front of the Saw-Horse during the escape, is slightly pricked by a knitting-needle, and ends up in the wide river.

l: the Soldier with the Green Whiskers, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Soldier with the Green Whiskers reaches the palace after the Emerald City is conquered and bars its doors and windows. He brings the Saw-Horse from the royal treasury and helps prepare the escape. He plans to disguise himself by cutting off his green whiskers and rides tied to the others into the river.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Scarecrow remains calm when told that the Emerald City has been conquered, but decides to escape after learning that the invading girls plan to destroy him. He chooses the Saw-Horse as their means of escape and plans to reach the Tin Woodman, then rides with Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Soldier toward the city gate. The Saw-Horse carries him into a wide river, where he is plunged beneath the current and floats like a cork.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: Jack Pumpkinhead tells Tip that the Saw-Horse carried him safely to the palace and worries that he may spoil if held prisoner. He rides behind Tip on the Saw-Horse, holding his pumpkin head firmly in place during the violent journey. He enters the wide river with the others and floats after being plunged beneath the current.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Saw-Horse is brought from the royal treasury after being fed a heaping peck of sawdust. It carries Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, the Scarecrow, and the Soldier through the palace gateway and charges through the invading girls, a fruit cart, several men, and the new Guardian of the Gate. It then races west and leaps into a wide river with its riders.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Tin Woodman rules over the Winkies and calls himself their Emperor. The Scarecrow intends to escape to him because he believes the Tin Woodman will protect him.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Emerald City is conquered by a regiment of girls from the four corners of the Land of Oz. Its walls and paving-stones are searched for emeralds by the invading army, and the Scarecrow’s group escapes from the city toward the west.

l: royal palace, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The palace is surrounded by the invading girls after the Emerald City is conquered. The Soldier bars its doors and windows, but an outer passage and gateway allow the Scarecrow’s group to escape.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The invading girls conquer the Emerald City and surround the palace. They guard the palace with knitting-needles, but the Saw-Horse knocks several over and carries the escaping prisoners past them.

l: Jinjur's takeover of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Emerald City is conquered by a regiment of girls, while the Standing Army runs because it cannot face the invaders’ weapons. The Scarecrow loses his throne but focuses on escaping because the conquerors intend to use his body for a rag carpet and sofa-cushions.

l: the escape from the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The Scarecrow, Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Soldier escape on the Saw-Horse after being tied together with a clothesline. They break through the palace gateway and the city gate, but their flight ends when the Saw-Horse leaps into a wide river.

l: the wide river, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Plans an escape
s: The wide river lies across the road west of the Emerald City. The Saw-Horse leaps into it without stopping, plunging the riders beneath the rapid current before they float on the surface like corks.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, the Scarecrow, and the Saw-Horse cross a river and reach the opposite bank. Jack’s pumpkin head floats away, but Tip retrieves it and replaces it, while he dries and repairs the Scarecrow. They resume their journey, recalling past adventures and heading to greet the Tin Woodman. At night, Tip sleeps on the grass while his companions keep watch because they do not sleep.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: Tip crosses the river on the Saw-Horse, retrieves Jack Pumpkinhead’s floating head, and helps repair both Jack and the Scarecrow. He mediates quarrels among his companions, then resumes the journey toward the Tin Woodman. At night, he is tired and hungry, so he sleeps on the grass using the Scarecrow as a pillow.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: The Saw-Horse floats because its wooden body is buoyant, paddles toward the opposite bank, and carries the travelers onward. It becomes offended by Jack’s remark that it sounds hoarse and quarrels with him, but continues the journey. It does not sleep and carries the group until Tip stops it for the night.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: Jack Pumpkinhead falls into the river, loses his pumpkin head, and is restored when Tip retrieves it from the water. He worries repeatedly that water, sunshine, insects, or other dangers might spoil his pumpkin, although his head is not cracked. He continues traveling with Tip, the Scarecrow, and the Saw-Horse.

l: His Majesty the Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: The Scarecrow is soaked during the river crossing, and his straw shifts into his legs while his wet crown crushes his face into wrinkles. Tip dries and reshapes him, restoring his usual appearance and balance. He recalls earlier adventures with Dorothy and helps keep the others from quarreling; he does not sleep.

l: river, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: The river causes the travelers to struggle during the crossing, but the Saw-Horse floats across it and reaches the opposite bank. Jack Pumpkinhead’s head becomes separated from him and floats downstream until Tip pulls it ashore.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: The Tin Woodman is identified by the Scarecrow as his friend Nick Chopper. The travelers are continuing their journey to greet him.

l: journey to the Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Journey to the Tin Woodman
s: The journey continues after Tip and his companions cross the river and recover from the damage caused by the water. They travel across the fields while the Scarecrow recalls past adventures, then stop at night so Tip can sleep. Their destination is the Tin Woodman.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: Tip, the Scarecrow, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse reach the Winkies’ capital and visit Nick Chopper, the Tin Woodman and Emperor of the Winkies. Nick Chopper is nickel-plated and welcomes the Scarecrow, though his putz-pomade rubs onto the Scarecrow before both are cleaned and polished. After learning that the girls of Oz have driven the Scarecrow from the Emerald City, Nick Chopper agrees to help recapture it. The group prepares for the journey and sets out toward the Emerald City, with Nick Chopper leading and the others accompanying him.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: Tip travels with the Scarecrow, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse to the City of the Winkies. He notices that Nick Chopper is made entirely of neatly soldered and riveted tin, and he tells Nick that the Saw-Horse was brought to life with magic powder. Tip mends Jack Pumpkinhead’s wooden limbs before the group begins its return journey to the Emerald City.

l: His Majesty the Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Scarecrow is pleased to see his old friend Nick Chopper, who is Emperor of the Winkies. Nick’s putz-pomade gets on the Scarecrow when they embrace, but the Scarecrow is later laundered, restuffed with his original brains, dressed in cleaned clothes, and given back his polished crown. He explains that the girls of Oz have driven him from the Emerald City, and he joins Nick’s effort to recapture it.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Saw-Horse carries Jack Pumpkinhead and accompanies Tip and the Scarecrow to the Winkies. Nick Chopper accepts it as a comrade after learning that it is alive and useful, and the Saw-Horse claims that it learns quickly. It is inspected before the group sets out toward the Emerald City.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: Nick Chopper is the Emperor of the Winkies and warmly welcomes the Scarecrow, Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse. He is composed entirely of tin, has a large heart, and bears an engraved star over the patch where the Wizard placed that heart. After hearing that the girls of Oz have taken the Emerald City, he decides to help the Scarecrow regain his throne and leads the group toward the city.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: Jack Pumpkinhead meets Nick Chopper and is invited to join the Emperor’s select society because he is unusual. He fears that his head will spoil, but Nick suggests that it can be canned and preserved. Tip strengthens Jack’s wooden limbs, and Jack rides the Saw-Horse on the return journey.

l: Winkies, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Winkies invited Nick Chopper to rule them after the Wicked Witch was destroyed. Their country is described as a kingdom, although Nick prefers the title Emperor, and a Lord High Chancellor is left to run it while Nick is away.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Emerald City has been captured by the girls of Oz after they drove the Scarecrow from his throne. Its treasury was robbed of all its jewels, and Nick Chopper and his companions set out to recapture the city.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The girls of Oz rise in revolt against the Scarecrow’s rule, saying that men have ruled the land long enough and that a poor rule does not work both ways. They drive the Scarecrow from the Emerald City, rob its treasury of jewels, and run the city themselves.

l: the Emperor's nickel-plating, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Emperor has himself nickel-plated because his tin body had become scratched during his adventures. The plating makes him shine magnificently after his servants polish him, and an engraved star on his breast covers the patch over his heart.

l: the Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The rebellion causes the girls of Oz to drive the Scarecrow from the Emerald City, seize the city, rob its treasury, and govern it themselves. Nick Chopper regards the rebellion as a calamity and agrees to oppose it.

l: Jinjur's takeover of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The girls of Oz capture the Emerald City after driving out the Scarecrow. They take all the jewels from its treasury and run the city to suit themselves, prompting Nick Chopper and the Scarecrow’s companions to plan its recapture.

l: Journey to the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: Nick Chopper, the Scarecrow, Tip, Jack Pumpkinhead, and the Saw-Horse begin the return journey to the Emerald City. Nick leads with his gleaming axe, while Jack rides the Saw-Horse and Tip and the Scarecrow walk beside him to keep Jack from falling or being damaged.

l: the Tin Woodman's nickel-plating, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Tin Woodman’s nickel-plating covers scratches from his adventures and gives his body a brilliant shine after polishing. An engraved star marks the location of his heart and conceals the patch made when the Wizard placed the heart in his breast.

l: Scarecrow's rule of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Nickel-Plated Emperor
s: The Scarecrow says that he cannot tell whether his subjects are happy because the girls of Oz have revolted and driven him from the Emerald City. He joins Nick Chopper’s plan to recapture the city and restore him to his throne.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: General Jinjur summons Mombi to help defend the Emerald City against the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman, while Mombi uses magic to obstruct their Journey to the Emerald City. The travelers encounter an illusory field of sunflowers, then lose their way and suffer the Saw-Horse's broken leg. They meet Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., a highly magnified and thoroughly educated insect, who agrees to relate his history.

l: General Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: General Jinjur, who commanded the Army of Revolt, becomes uneasy when the Scarecrow escapes from the Emerald City. She summons Mombi and promises her large rewards for helping the rebel army defeat the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The Army of Revolt is endangered by the escape of the Scarecrow and the possibility that he will join forces with the Tin Woodman. General Jinjur seeks Mombi's assistance against them.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The Scarecrow travels with the Tin Woodman, Tip, Jack, and the Saw-Horse toward the Emerald City. He recognizes that the landscape has been altered, proposes using the sun as a guide, and politely questions Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., about his name and education.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The Tin Woodman realizes that the travelers have lost their way when they reach an unfamiliar field of sunflowers. He refuses to chop down the apparently living flowers, helps save Jack's pumpkin, and later considers how to replace the Saw-Horse's broken leg.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Mombi is furious with Tip for escaping and taking the Powder of Life, so she agrees to help General Jinjur. After reaching the royal palace, she uses secret magic from a locked room in a tower to prevent the Scarecrow and his companions from returning.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Tip identifies the sunflower field as witchcraft and suspects that Mombi is creating an illusion. He leads the group through it by having Jack ride forward while he follows the Saw-Horse with his eyes closed, and he later replaces Jack's pumpkin after the Saw-Horse falls.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The Emerald City is under General Jinjur's control when Mombi arrives at its royal palace. Mombi works there to prevent the Scarecrow and his companions from returning.

l: Journey to the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: During the Journey to the Emerald City, the travelers encounter Mombi's altered landscape, including a confusing field of sunflowers. They use the sun to keep their direction but are delayed when the Saw-Horse breaks a leg.

l: witchcraft, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Witchcraft creates or appears to create the field of sunflowers and changes the appearance of the landscape. Tip attributes these obstacles to Mombi's magic, while the Scarecrow notes that the sun cannot be changed and therefore remains a reliable guide.

l: field of sunflowers, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The travelers find themselves surrounded by a field of tall, rapidly whirling sunflowers whose vivid red and gold colors dazzle them. When they proceed with their eyes closed, the field disappears without a trace.

l: sunflowers, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The sunflowers have gigantic flowers that whirl like miniature windmills. Their centers briefly show girls' faces that laugh at the travelers, but Tip believes the flowers are an illusion.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: The Saw-Horse falls into a rabbit hole, sending Jack into the air, and one of its legs breaks when it is pulled free. It feels no pain but says that its pride is injured because its anatomy is brittle.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Jack rides the Saw-Horse through the sunflower illusion and announces when the way is clear. He is thrown into the air when the Saw-Horse falls, but the Tin Woodman catches his pumpkin, and Tip replaces it on his neck.

l: Woggle-Bug, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., approaches the travelers and presents a card bearing his name. He explains that H. M. means Highly Magnified and T. E. means Thoroughly Educated; he is a large, formally dressed insect who offers to relate his history.

l: Woggle-Bug's history, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E.
s: Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T. E., says he will relate his history so the travelers can understand his unusual appearance. The unit ends as he begins to tell the story, without giving its contents.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Woggle-Bug recounts how Professor Nowitall captured him, projected him in a highly magnified state with a magnifying-glass, and accidentally enabled his escape from the school house. He joins the Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Saw-Horse, Pumpkinhead, and Tip on their journey toward the Emerald City. The Woggle-Bug helps solve the Saw-Horse’s broken-leg problem by suggesting that Pumpkinhead’s wooden leg be reshaped for the repair.

l: Woggle-Bug, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Woggle-Bug explains that he was once an ordinary insect but became thoroughly educated by listening to Professor Nowitall’s lessons for years. After being projected in a highly magnified state, he escaped the school house and later acquired clothing from a grateful tailor. He joins the company traveling toward the Emerald City and suggests how to repair the Saw-Horse.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Scarecrow says that education is something to be proud of and that the brains given to him by the Great Wizard are considered unexcelled. He admires the Woggle-Bug’s clever repair suggestion and directs the Tin Woodman to use Pumpkinhead’s leg to fix the Saw-Horse.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Tin Woodman argues that a good heart is more desirable than education or brains. He amputates Pumpkinhead’s left leg and whittles it down to fit the Saw-Horse, then helps lead the company toward the Emerald City.

l: Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Saw-Horse has a broken leg and cannot travel until it is repaired. It receives Pumpkinhead’s reshaped wooden leg, though it complains that the new leg is a disgrace and insults Pumpkinhead.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Pumpkinhead asks whether seeds could be considered brains and is told by Tip to keep quiet. Because his joints are stiff, he must ride the Saw-Horse; he gives up his left leg so it can be reshaped into a replacement leg for the horse, and he quarrels with the Saw-Horse afterward.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Tip tells Pumpkinhead to keep quiet and later points out that insects do not normally wear clothes. He explains that the group cannot leave because the Saw-Horse is injured and Pumpkinhead must ride.

l: Professor Nowitall, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Professor Nowitall is described as the most famous scholar in the Land of Oz. He discovers the Woggle-Bug, captures him, and uses a magnifying-glass to project him onto a screen for his students to study.

l: Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Land of Oz is described as the place where Professor Nowitall is the most famous scholar. The Woggle-Bug plans to visit the Emerald City within the Land of Oz.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Woggle-Bug intends to visit the Emerald City to give lectures on the Advantages of Magnification. The Scarecrow’s company is already traveling toward the Emerald City and invites the Woggle-Bug to join them.

l: magnifying-glass, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Professor Nowitall brings a curious magnifying-glass from a cupboard and uses it to project the Woggle-Bug onto a screen in a highly magnified state.

l: education, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Woggle-Bug gains education by listening attentively to Professor Nowitall’s lectures for about three years. He takes pride in being Thoroughly Educated, while the Scarecrow says that education is something to be proud of.

l: magnification, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Magnification transforms the Woggle-Bug from a tiny insect into a creature large enough to travel safely and associate with learned people. The Woggle-Bug plans to lecture in the Emerald City on the Advantages of Magnification.

l: Woggle-Bug’s escape from the school house, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: After the Woggle-Bug’s bow frightens two girls and causes the school room to empty, he remains alone in a highly magnified state. He walks out of the school house, turns a corner, and escapes unnoticed into a nearby grove of trees.

l: Woggle-Bug’s capture and projection, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: Professor Nowitall catches the Woggle-Bug between his thumb and forefinger after discovering him crawling across the hearth. He projects the Woggle-Bug onto a screen in a highly magnified state so the students can study his construction and habits.

l: repair of the Saw-Horse, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Woggle-Bug suggests using one of Pumpkinhead’s wooden legs to replace the Saw-Horse’s broken leg. The Tin Woodman amputates and reshapes Pumpkinhead’s left leg, and the one-legged Pumpkinhead is tied onto the repaired Saw-Horse.

l: Journey to the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, A Highly Magnified History
s: The Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Saw-Horse, Pumpkinhead, and Tip resume their journey toward the Emerald City after repairing the Saw-Horse. The Woggle-Bug accepts their invitation and travels with them.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Tip and his companions travel toward the Emerald City while Old Mombi uses deceptive magic to obstruct them. The Queen of the Field Mice guides them and sends twelve Field Mice to hide in the Scarecrow so they can help him regain his throne. Mombi's illusions include a river, a granite wall, spinning roads, and a sheet of flame, but the travelers pass through them safely by following the Queen. The group reaches the gates of the Emerald City, and the Queen returns home.

l: Mombi, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Old Mombi uses witchcraft to create deceptive obstacles that try to prevent Tip and his companions from reaching the Emerald City. Her illusions include a rushing river, a granite wall, whirling roads, and a sheet of flame.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Tip travels with the Scarecrow and the others toward the Emerald City. He is the only member of the party who becomes tired and must repeatedly stop to rest.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: The Scarecrow asks the Queen of the Field Mice for twelve subjects to help him regain his throne. He hides the twelve Field Mice in the straw inside his body and plans to release them in the Emerald City.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: The Tin Woodman chops down the Saw-Horse's new leg when it proves too long. He summons the Queen of the Field Mice, asks her to guide the party, and recognizes that the apparent fire is only a deception.

l: Queen of the Field Mice, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: The Queen agrees to provide the Scarecrow with twelve subjects and then guides the travelers toward the Emerald City. She passes safely through each of Mombi's illusions, enabling the others to follow, and departs after they reach the city's gates.

l: Field Mice, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Twelve Field Mice obey their Queen and hide in the straw inside the Scarecrow. They are intended to rush out in the Emerald City and help the Scarecrow regain his throne.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: The travelers reach the gates of the Emerald City after overcoming the magical obstacles that seemed to block their route. The Scarecrow intends to regain his throne there.

l: witchcraft, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Magic is described by the Scarecrow as unnatural and therefore something to be feared and avoided. In this unit, magic creates convincing but harmless deceptions that disappear or have no physical effect.

l: Mombi's magical obstacles, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: Mombi's magical obstacles are deceptive appearances rather than real barriers. The travelers pass through a seeming river, a granite wall, and shifting roads, while the Queen of the Field Mice guides them safely onward.

l: sheet of illusory flame, The Marvelous Land of Oz, Old Mombi indulges in Witchcraft
s: The sheet of illusory flame rushes across the meadow and frightens the travelers, who fear being burned. The Queen walks through it unharmed, revealing that it is only a deception, and the others follow without being scorched.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, Tip, and their companions enter the Emerald City to restore the Scarecrow to the throne, but General Jinjur and the Army of Revolt capture them in the throne room. The Tin Woodman frightens the guards at the gateway, yet the apparent ease of their progress proves to be a trap. General Jinjur orders the nonhuman prisoners destroyed, but the Scarecrow releases mice that panic the Army of Revolt and drive it from the palace. The Scarecrow's party bars the palace entrances and gathers in the throne room to plan what to do next.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Scarecrow enters the Emerald City with his friends to reclaim his throne and becomes uneasy when the Army of Revolt offers no resistance. After General Jinjur captures him, he releases mice from inside his jacket, causing the rebels to flee, and then helps secure the palace.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Tin Woodman frightens the girls guarding the gateway by swinging his axe and leads the party into the city. General Jinjur's forces later snatch his axe from him, leaving him disarmed and helpless, but he escapes when the mice panic the rebels.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: Tip travels with the Scarecrow's party into the Emerald City and warns that their unopposed progress is too easy and may conceal trouble. He is included among the prisoners whom General Jinjur intends to restore to old Mombi.

l: General Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: General Jinjur sits in the Scarecrow's throne wearing his second-best crown and holding the royal sceptre, claiming that the throne belongs to whoever can take it. After the Scarecrow's party is captured, she orders most of them destroyed, but mice frighten her into fleeing the palace and continuing to the city gates.

l: Army of Revolt, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Army of Revolt controls the Emerald City and initially allows the Scarecrow's party to advance without opposition. It surrounds the party in the throne room, but its members flee in terror when the Scarecrow releases mice.

l: the party of prisoners, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Scarecrow's party enters the Emerald City and reaches the royal palace without resistance before being surrounded and captured by the Army of Revolt. It escapes when mice panic the rebels, then bars the palace entrances and gathers for a council of war.

l: Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Emerald City is under the control of the women and the Army of Revolt after the revolution. The Scarecrow's party enters it and advances toward the royal palace while the city's women largely watch, laugh, or step aside.

l: gateway of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The gateway of the Emerald City is guarded by two girls from the Army of Revolt carrying knitting-needles. The Tin Woodman frightens them away with his swinging axe, allowing the travelers to enter.

l: royal palace, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The royal palace has marble steps from which the Army of Revolt has torn the emeralds, leaving tiny holes. After the mouse panic, the Scarecrow's party closes, bolts, and locks its entrances against the returning rebels.

l: throne room, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The throne room contains General Jinjur seated on the Scarecrow's throne with his crown and the royal sceptre. The Army of Revolt captures the Scarecrow's party there, but the room is deserted when the mice send the rebels fleeing, and the party later uses it for a council of war.

l: revolution, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The revolution placed the women in control of the Emerald City after the Scarecrow left. Men are described as performing housework and minding children while the women run things to suit themselves.

l: capture of the Scarecrow's party, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Army of Revolt captures the Scarecrow's party in the throne room after General Jinjur signals the rebels and the Tin Woodman's axe is snatched away. General Jinjur then announces that the prisoners will be destroyed, except for Tip, who will be returned to old Mombi.

l: mouse panic, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The mouse panic begins when the Scarecrow releases several mice from inside his jacket. The mice cause the Army of Revolt and General Jinjur to flee the throne room and abandon the palace.

l: Tin Woodman's axe, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Tin Woodman uses his axe to frighten the guards at the gateway and clear a path into the Emerald City. In the throne room, someone behind him snatches the axe from his grasp, leaving him disarmed.

l: knitting-needles, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The girls guarding the gateway draw knitting-needles from their hair and threaten to prod anyone who approaches. The Army of Revolt later carries the glistening knitting-needles in both hands while surrounding the prisoners.

l: mice, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: The Scarecrow releases a succession of tiny grey mice from his bosom. Their presence terrifies the Army of Revolt and General Jinjur, enabling the prisoners to escape.

l: women's rule of the Emerald City, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: Under the women's rule, men in the Emerald City sweep, dust, wash dishes, and mind children while women sit gossiping and laughing. The women and the Army of Revolt show little concern when the Scarecrow's party enters the city.

l: prisoners' planned destruction, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Prisoners of the Queen
s: General Jinjur plans to chop up the Saw-Horse and Jack Pumpkinhead's body for kindling, use the pumpkin to make tarts, burn the Scarecrow, cut the Tin Woodman into pieces for the goats, and make the Woggle-Bug into soup or goulash. Tip is excluded from this plan because he belongs to old Mombi and is to be returned to her.

l: The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: The Scarecrow realizes that Jinjur remains Queen and that he and his companions are prisoners in her palace, which is surrounded by girl soldiers. After learning about Tip’s nearly exhausted Powder of Life, he thinks of escaping through the air rather than through the guarded doors or underground. He proposes that Nick Chopper build a winged machine on the palace roof and that Tip bring it to life with the powder. Nick repairs Jack Pumpkinhead’s damaged leg, and the companions begin gathering materials for the aerial machine.

l: Scarecrow, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: The Scarecrow acknowledges that Jinjur is still Queen and that the group remains imprisoned in her palace. After thinking quietly, he proposes escaping through the air in a winged machine brought to life by Tip’s Powder of Life, and he removes his heavy crown as his last memento of royalty.

l: General Jinjur, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: Jinjur continues to claim the throne and remains Queen after the group’s failed attempt to defeat her. She surrounds the palace with girl soldiers and has threatened to make tarts, soup, or goulash from members of the group.

l: Woggle-Bug, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: The Woggle-Bug argues that the Scarecrow was King before Jinjur arrived and fears being turned into goulash or soup. He becomes distressed by the others’ discussion of eating the group’s members and helps Nick Chopper set Jack Pumpkinhead on his new leg.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: Jack Pumpkinhead fears that Jinjur will make tarts of him and worries that he will decay. After asking to be released from the Saw-Horse, he receives a carved mahogany table leg from Nick Chopper and is able to walk and help with the escape effort.

l: Tip, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: Tip confirms that Jinjur’s soldiers surround the palace and explains that his nearly exhausted Powder of Life can bring things to life. He agrees to use the powder on the winged machine and helps remove the Scarecrow’s crown.

l: Tin Woodman, The Marvelous Land of Oz, The Scarecrow Takes Time to Think
s: Nick Chopper agrees that Jinjur remains Queen and that the group is still her prisoner. As a skilled mechanic, he accepts the task of building a winged escape machine and repairs Jack Pumpkinhead by fitting him with a mahogany table leg.
